title: Recognising and treating coccidiosis in young chicks
subtitle: Coccidiosis kills brooder chicks quickly. Bloody droppings and huddling in a warm chick that was fine yesterday are the signal to act that day.
excerpt: Coccidiosis is a parasitic gut infection caused by Eimeria species. It strikes chicks between 3 and 12 weeks, often in wet bedding or overcrowded brooder conditions. The first sign is usually a chick that looks puffed up and stops eating; bloody droppings follow within hours. Treatment with amprolium in the water works if started early.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Laying Hens. AHDB Poultry, coccidiosis management factsheet. Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive, chapter on poultry diseases. University of Wisconsin Extension, raising baby chicks.

glossaryTerms.definition: A parasitic infection of the intestinal lining caused by Eimeria protozoa. Spreads through faecal contamination of bedding and water. Causes bloody or mucoid droppings, puffed-up posture, reduced appetite, and death in severe cases.
An antiprotozoal drug used to treat coccidiosis in poultry. It blocks thiamine uptake in the coccidia parasite. Administered in drinking water for 3–7 days.
The resilient microscopic egg of the Eimeria parasite, shed in faeces. Survives in soil and bedding for over a year. The main transmission route for coccidiosis.

content.text: deteriorates fast. A chick that looks puffed and quiet in the morning may be dead by evening if the case is severe. The disease progresses in a wave through a brooder, expect to see several birds affected within 24 hours of the first showing symptoms.
Puffed-up posture, feathers fluffed, chick standing hunched.
Wet, mucoid droppings with no blood in milder cases (some Eimeria species do not cause haemorrhage).
Reduced activity and appetite. Chick stands by heat source rather than moving around.
in wet bedding are the main reinfection source. Replace with fresh dry bedding.
Remove and discard any standing water. Clean and disinfect drinkers before refilling.
treatment in the water immediately. Dosage: follow the label rate on the product (typically 1 ml per litre for the treatment dose). Treat the whole brooder, not just the visibly ill birds.
Continue treatment for 5-7 days. Replace medicated water every 24 hours.

Raise the heat slightly if the chicks are huddling. A severely affected chick may be too weak to maintain its own temperature. Offer electrolytes in a second drinker alongside the medicated water, coccidiosis causes fluid loss and weakness.

The three conditions that trigger coccidiosis outbreaks are wet bedding, overcrowding, and stress. A brooder that is changed daily, has adequate space per chick (at least 0.1 m² per chick to six weeks), and uses a nipple drinker rather than an open dish has much lower coccidiosis rates.
Medicated chick crumbs with amprolium are sold as a prevention. The low dose builds resistance over time. If you use medicated crumbs, do not also add full-dose amprolium to the water.
